findings.evidence: `pkg/parser/charset/encoding_gb18030.go:86` implements `(*encodingGB18030).MbLen`; its 4-byte branch reads `bs[2]` and `bs[3]` without checking `len(bs) >= 4` (`pkg/parser/charset/encoding_gb18030.go:95`). `MbLen` is called from lexer `skipRune` on the remaining suffix `r.s[r.p.Offset:]` with no length guard (`pkg/parser/lexer.go:1100`).
findings.fix: Guard the 4-byte check with a length condition, e.g. `if len(bs) >= 4 && 0x30 <= bs[1] ... && 0x30 <= bs[3] ... { return 4 }`, so truncated/invalid prefixes safely return 0 instead of panicking (consistent with `peek()` which already checks `length < 4`).
findings.impact: A malformed/truncated GB18030 4-byte prefix at end-of-input (e.g., bytes `[0x81..0xFE, 0x30..0x39]` with only 2–3 bytes remaining) can trigger an out-of-bounds panic during lexing of quoted identifiers or string literals. This is a robustness/security risk (potential DoS) when the SQL text contains invalid GB18030 byte sequences.
findings.later_fix_evidence: Checked `upstream/master` (at `3b531d4e3d99cb988bebccb8f63a96afff0ec6cd`): `pkg/parser/charset/encoding_gb18030.go` still has the same unguarded `bs[2]`/`bs[3]` access in `MbLen`.
findings.verify: Add a unit test that calls `EncodingGB18030Impl.MbLen(string([]byte{0x81,0x30}))` and `MbLen(string([]byte{0x81,0x30,0x81}))` and asserts it returns 0 (and does not panic). Add a parser/lexer test that scans a string/identifier containing those trailing bytes under client charset `gb18030` and asserts it returns a parse/invalid-encoding error rather than panicking.
findings.what: `encodingGB18030.MbLen` can panic on short inputs: it indexes `bs[2]`/`bs[3]` when the second byte looks like a 4-byte sequence prefix, without ensuring at least 4 bytes are available.

subject: charset,collation: implement `GB18030` and 2 collations (#55792)
